item.title: U20 youth training hard ahead of TISA Cup Tournament
item.description: Kolomotu’a’s young men and women are stepping up their preparations for an upcoming local rugby tournament, and were training hard at at Halaano Rugby Field on Friday. Hosted by Kolomotu'a, the TISA Insurance Kolomotu'a Under-20s and Women's XV 2026 Tournament will run for 11 weeks, beginning on August 29, with the finals scheduled for November 7.
item.content:encoded:
Kolomotu’a’s young men and women are stepping up their preparations for an upcoming local rugby tournament, and were training hard at at Halaano Rugby Field on Friday.

Hosted by Kolomotu'a, the TISA Insurance Kolomotu'a Under-20s and Women's XV 2026 Tournament will run for 11 weeks, beginning on August 29, with the finals scheduled for November 7.

Head coach Taliai Taufa said rugby was more than a sport for young people, providing an opportunity to develop skills, confidence and a passion for the game.

“I see the kids playing and it is more than just a sport. They really enjoy playing rugby and we try to teach them the practical skills as well as keeping their interests and passion.”

Taufa said it was important for young players to be encouraged to participate and enjoy the game rather than focusing solely on performance.

“Rugby is not just a sport or a career path, it is also something they can just enjoy. There is no special qualification needed to play rugby,” he said.

The training continued under cloudy and windy conditions yesterday, with players working through drills covering different aspects of rugby.

A young player said rugby had become something she looked forward to each day.

“I get tired but playing beside the other girls is something I enjoy so much. I look forward to our evening trainings every day,” she said.

Coaches said more young women were taking up rugby, with participation growing as traditional perceptions that rugby was primarily a men's sport continued to change.

Women's rugby has become increasingly popular in Tonga, with four women's teams confirmed for this year's competition.

TISA Insurance Kolomotu'a Under-20s and Women's XV 2026

Nine men's teams and four women's teams have been confirmed for the 11 weeks competition. The tournament draw has been completed ahead of the opening round on 29 August.

The men's teams are Marist 'Apifo'ou, Fasi Ma'ufanga, Houmakelikao, Ngele'ia Warlords, Havelu Bulldogs, Hihifo, Toloa Old Boys, Hasini Roosters and Kolomotu'a Eagles.

The women's teams are Kolofo'ou Lioness, Havelu Bulldogs, Hihifo and Kolomotu'a Eagles.

These teams are also holding regular trainings in their villages in preparation for what will be the last rugby tournament of the year on Tongatapu

item.title: Crossbow importer given suspended two-year prison sentence
item.description: Langima’a Lausi’i has been sentenced to two years’ imprisonment, fully suspended for three years, after importing a tactical crossbow, steel balls and arrows from the United States without declaring them or obtaining an import licence. item.content:encoded:
Langima’a Lausi’i has been sentenced to two years’ imprisonment, fully suspended for three years, after importing a tactical crossbow, steel balls and arrows from the United States without declaring them or obtaining an import licence.

Hon. Justice Targowski sentenced Lausi’i on 7 August at the Supreme Court in Nuku’alofa after he pleaded guilty in May to three charges, including failing to declare the prohibited goods.

The case arose on 28 May 2025 when an 8x4 box from the United States arrived in Tonga aboard the Olomana V169 and was searched by Customs officers at SF Enterprises as part of the routine release process.

Lausi’i, the importer, completed an authorisation form with Customs broker Nesi Mafi. When asked whether the box contained illicit items such as firearms or ammunition, he said it did not.

Customs officer Sione ‘Aho initially scanned the box and found nothing unusual. However, when it was opened, officers found a white case containing undeclared prohibited items, including a WT4 Tactical Crossbow and arrows.

When questioned, Lausi’i said he considered the items to be toys and did not believe they needed to be declared.

Further inspection revealed the box had a double floor, beneath which Customs officers found additional steel ball ammunition. Police were notified, and Lausi’i was told that an import licence was required. He said arrows were allowed in the United States, but was informed that a licence was required to import them into Tonga.

The items were confiscated and Lausi’i arrested. It was confirmed that he had neither an import licence nor applied for one.

The court heard that the WT4 Tactical Crossbow is considered an “arm” under the Arms and Ammunition Act, and that the crossbow, steel balls and arrows were all in usable condition.

Justice Targowski described the importation of the crossbow as a serious offence, noting that the maximum penalty under the Act is 10 years’ imprisonment.

He adopted previous judicial comments that unlawful importation of firearms and ammunition had become a greater threat to society and that such offences should generally start with imprisonment rather than a fine.

The judge set a starting point of three years’ imprisonment but reduced the sentence by 12 months because Lausi’i pleaded guilty at the earliest opportunity and cooperated with police.

In considering whether to suspend the sentence, the judge noted that Lausi’i had no previous convictions, had pleaded guilty early, cooperated with police, and had a serious physical disability. He was also self-employed and had a low income, making a fine inappropriate.

Lausi’i was therefore sentenced to two years’ imprisonment, fully suspended for three years.

The conditions require him to remain on probation, not commit any punishable offence, complete 80 hours of community service and undertake a life skills course as directed by Probation.

Justice Targowski warned that any breach of the conditions could result in the suspended sentence being activated in full.

The seized goods were ordered to be forfeited to the Crown.
